title: Apply routine maintenance and servicing plans and procedures

lessons.title: Maintenance plans and schedules
lessons.html:
Why routine maintenance?

Breakdowns during planting, spraying or harvest are costly: work stops, crops suffer, and emergency repairs are expensive. Routine (preventive) maintenance keeps equipment and infrastructure in safe working order, extends its life and reduces costs.

Types of maintenance

  • Daily checks: done by the operator before use.
  • Scheduled servicing: at set hours, kilometres or calendar intervals according to the manufacturer's manual (e.g. oil and filter changes).
  • Seasonal maintenance: preparing planters before planting, sprayers before spraying season, and storing equipment after the season.
  • Corrective repairs: fixing faults found during checks or after breakdowns.

The maintenance plan

A maintenance plan lists each asset and what must be done, when and by whom. A simple example:

AssetTaskIntervalResponsible
Tractor 3Pre-start checkDailyOperator
Tractor 3Engine oil and filterPer manual hoursWorkshop
Boom sprayerNozzle check and calibrationStart of season and regularlySpray supervisor
Borehole pumpCheck flow and electricsMonthlyMaintenance team
Fences, troughsInspectionWeeklyStock team

The manufacturer's manual

The operator's manual gives service intervals, oil types and quantities, grease points, tyre pressures and safety instructions. Always follow it; using the wrong oil or skipping a service can damage engines and void warranties.

Hour meters and logbooks

Track hours or kilometres on each machine. Record fuel, services, repairs and parts in a logbook or the farm's maintenance system so the next service is never missed.

lessons.title: Carrying out servicing procedures safely
lessons.html:
Daily pre-start checks for a tractor

  • Engine oil, coolant and hydraulic oil levels
  • Fuel level and any leaks under the machine
  • Air filter condition (especially in dusty conditions)
  • Tyre pressure and damage; wheel nuts
  • Lights, indicators, brakes, horn and seatbelt
  • PTO guards and shields in place
  • Grease points as specified

Record the check and report faults before using the machine. Never use a machine with faulty brakes, steering or missing guards.

General servicing steps

  1. Park on level ground, lower implements, engage the parking brake.
  2. Switch off the engine, remove the key and keep it with you. Tag the machine "Do not operate" if needed.
  3. Let hot parts cool before working on them.
  4. Use the correct tools, parts and lubricants listed in the manual.
  5. Support raised machinery on proper stands; never work under a load held only by hydraulics or a jack.
  6. Replace guards and covers when done.
  7. Test run, check for leaks and record the work.

Implements and equipment

  • Planters: check seed plates, chains, discs and tyre pressures before planting.
  • Sprayers: clean filters and nozzles, check hoses and pressure gauges, calibrate. Wear PPE because residues remain.
  • Pumps and irrigation: clean filters, flush lines, check for leaks.
  • Hand tools: sharpen, oil and store dry.

Waste and environment

Collect used oil, filters and coolant in marked containers for recycling or approved disposal. Clean spills with absorbent material. Never pour oil onto soil or into drains.

Safety and the law

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires employers to provide and maintain safe machinery and to train workers. Only trained, authorised people may service machines. Wear overalls, safety boots, gloves and eye protection.

Key points

  • Follow the maintenance plan and the manufacturer's manual.
  • Do daily pre-start checks and report faults before use.
  • Switch off, remove the key and support machinery before servicing.
  • Record all services and repairs in a logbook.
  • Dispose of oil and filters properly.
